Foundation 18: IGameComponent, IGraphicsDeviceManager, IEffectMatrices, IEffectFog as Ruby modules whose members raise NotImplementedError; 4 types / 11 Ruby identities. Foundation 20: one CLR public event projects to one public Ruby event reader keeping the XNA spelling, answering the generic CNA::Runtime::Event subscription primitive whose whole public surface is add/remove. Registration-ordered dispatch over a snapshot, duplicate subscriptions permitted, last-occurrence removal matching Delegate.Remove, exceptions never swallowed, raising internal to the declaring implementation. System.EventArgs projects as CNA::Runtime::EventArgs with only its two public CLR identities. Verifier measures kind event under EVENT_MAPPING_MISMATCH with EVENT_IDENTITIES=6 across three owner types; mutation coverage rejects add_/remove_ pairs, writers, wrong support types, extra identities and any public emit/fire/trigger surface. No add_EventName or remove_EventName identity and no fabricated ::System namespace exists

Foundation 35: GameComponentCollection, the sealed Collection<IGameComponent> Game.Components is; 1 type / 7 Ruby identities -- one constructor, four protected hooks and two events -- with the whole Collection<T> public surface arriving by inheritance from CNA::Runtime::Collection, which Foundation 34 projected from the admitted mscorlib. Derived from the pinned Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Game.dll IL: InsertItem refuses a duplicate before mutating and raises ComponentAdded after, RemoveItem reads before mutating and raises ComponentRemoved after, ClearItems raises every ComponentRemoved before any mutation while re-reading Count, and SetItem is an unconditional NotSupportedException. A null component is inserted silently because the IL null check guards the notification rather than the mutation. This capability holds no component: no concrete IGameComponent type exists yet and nothing populates one

Foundation 39: the IL inventory records, per type, every call/callvirt/newobj/ldftn/ldvirtftn/jmp edge that lands on a pinned reference type other than its owner -- 3271 edges across 257 types, from the same operands the native-reachability fixpoint already collected and with the same normalisation. Purely additive: TYPES_NATIVE_REACHABLE stays 77, NATIVE_ENTRY_POINT_METHODS stays 254 and no prior per-type fact moved. The frontier consumes it in two new reports and relaxes no policy: dependencyCompleteCandidates stays 19, consumableCandidates stays 0, the blocker summary is identical and selectedNext is still nil. It settles two questions the signature graph structurally cannot answer -- whether a dependency on a partial type is really unmet, member for member, and whether a type's IL reaches a type no public signature names. GameComponent reaches exactly one Game member, get_Components, which is complete, so Foundation 38's selection is proved rather than asserted; DrawableGameComponent reaches nine members of IGraphicsDeviceService, a missing type, and its Initialize throws InvalidOperationException(MissingGraphicsDeviceService) without a registered producer, so it is held back rather than looking ready; six candidates the signature graph called dependency-complete are exposed as blocked by a type only their IL reaches

Foundation 38: GameComponent, 1 type / 14 Ruby identities, the first concrete component this binding ships. Pure managed -- the IL inventory records it nativeReachable false with no native entry point -- and it really includes the IGameComponent and IUpdateable modules, which is what Game's engine tests with is_a?. Measured from the pinned Game.dll: the constructor has no null check, so a component with no Game is legal; enabled defaults true as a field initialiser and updateOrder to the CLR default 0; both setters suppress a same-value write first and write the field before raising, so a handler always observes the new value; OnEnabledChanged and OnUpdateOrderChanged declare a sender parameter and ignore it, raising with the component itself; Initialize and Update are bare rets. Dispose removes the component from Game.Components before raising Disposed, both under a reentrant lock, and the type carries no disposed flag at all, so disposing twice raises Disposed twice. Dispose(false) returns at its first instruction and Finalize is exactly that call, so the CLR finalizer does nothing observable; no ObjectSpace finalizer is registered anywhere in this binding and no GC.SuppressFinalize analogue was invented, because there is nothing to suppress. The two Dispose overloads project to one Ruby method dispatching on arity, which widens the protected overload to public -- recorded as a mapping limitation Ruby cannot avoid. Game.Dispose disposes each component over a snapshot copy. DrawableGameComponent stays deferred on Graphics.GraphicsDevice

Foundation 37: Game.Components and Game.Services, the first two members any deferred partial runtime type has closed. Both are pure managed state -- each getter is one ldfld, each answers the same object for the life of the Game, neither goes through the C ABI and neither needs a native host, so both work on a Game that has never run. Services is allocated in the constructor's field-initialiser prologue and Components after the base constructor, which is the order the pinned Game.dll .ctor performs; the two collection handlers are subscribed immediately afterwards. Behind them the private engine is implemented exactly: BinarySearch with the CLR's own comparers, which answer 0 only for an equal component and so behave as a lower bound, followed by the forward walk that makes insertion stable among equal orders; order-changed subscription on insertion and unsubscription on removal; the notYetInitialized queue, drained by Game.Initialize with Count re-read and the element removed after its Initialize returns. Game.Update and Game.Draw carry their exact base bodies over a snapshot list, reading Enabled and Visible at call time. Ruby class inheritance is the whole base-call mechanism: no GameBaseUpdate-style helper exists, the native host invokes the virtual method once and never runs the base itself, and a subclass that omits super really suppresses the base component pass. Not implemented and recorded: the FrameworkDispatcher.Update the base Update performs, because the CNA game loop already drives that pump every frame and this binding's dispatcher projection requires a live Game; the device-event hookup and the conditional LoadContent in the base Initialize, both guarded by an IGraphicsDeviceService this binding has no key for; and LaunchParameters, ContentManager and GameWindow, each a missing type. Nothing registers a service and no component type ships yet

Foundation 36: System.IDisposable projects to no Ruby constant at all, the second recorded structural collapse after System.IServiceProvider and the first with real reach. The admitted mscorlib shows the interface declares exactly one member, void Dispose(), and nothing else; twenty-nine XNA types declare it, twenty-eight declare a public parameterless Dispose of their own, and GraphicsDeviceManager implements it explicitly, which projects to no member under the rule ReadOnlyCollection and Collection already follow. No IDisposable or Disposable module, no Close alias, no IsDisposed of this projection's own, no finalizer API and no ownership wrapper exists; the verifier catches an invented constant under LANGUAGE_MAPPING_MISMATCH, a module inside the XNA namespaces as an INTERNAL_TYPE_LEAK, and a Close alias on a projected type as an UNEXPECTED_MEMBER. It claims no type's disposal is implemented: Audio.SoundEffectInstance and Audio.Cue lose their BCL blocker and keep NATIVE_RUNTIME, so no XACT runtime is claimed and neither becomes consumable

Foundation 21: CNA::Runtime::BclProjection is the measured register of non-XNA CLR identities this binding projects — System.EventArgs to CNA::Runtime::EventArgs, and System.Exception and System.Runtime.InteropServices.ExternalException to the Ruby StandardError root. The API verifier resolves and shape-checks every entry under LANGUAGE_MAPPING_MISMATCH and the dependency frontier consumes the same register, so no BCL type can be reported as mapped that the runtime does not project. StandardError rather than ::Exception because a CLR catch (Exception) is the analogue of a bare Ruby rescue; an intermediate BCL exception class the XNA surface never names collapses to the nearest projected ancestor. System.Type, IServiceProvider, IO.Stream, TimeSpan as a first-class type, Attribute, StringBuilder, SerializationInfo, ReadOnlyCollection and Dictionary are deliberately not designed

Foundation 22: six XNA exception types as real Ruby exceptions rooted at StandardError - Audio InstancePlayLimitException, NoAudioHardwareException, NoMicrophoneConnectedException; Graphics DeviceLostException, DeviceNotResetException, NoSuitableGraphicsDeviceException; 6 types / 18 Ruby identities. The pinned IL shows all eight XNA exception types declare zero fields, zero methods and four constructors whose entire body is a pure forward to the CLR exception base, with no message synthesis and no validation. The inner exception maps to Ruby Exception#cause, bound at construction with the backtrace cleared, so an unraised exception matches the CLR's InnerException set and StackTrace null. ContentLoadException and StorageDeviceNotConnectedException stay deferred on System.Runtime.Serialization. Nothing in this binding raises any of them, there is no audio engine, and Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Storage does not exist; Foundation 27 later opened the Content namespace for the five ContentSerializer attributes

Foundation 22: the original Microsoft XNA Framework 4.0 Windows assemblies are on this host and are located by exact SHA-256, never by filename. tools/api_compat/reference/XNA_IL_PROVENANCE.md pins ten of them by hash, size and version, including the two the behaviour corpus had cited since Milestone 3. tools/api_compat/build_il_inventory.rb admits each by hash, refuses to run on any mismatch, disassembles with ikdasm and writes docs/generated/xna-il-inventory.json: declaring assembly, IL size, declared field and method counts, per-constructor access and pure-base-forward proof, and native reachability. Native frontier 2 corrected the extractor and all 257 of 257 reference types have IL. No Microsoft-owned bytes and no machine-local path is committed, and the gem packages zero Microsoft binaries

Foundation 28: a Microsoft .NET Framework 4.0 mscorlib is admitted as a SEPARATE BCL authority beside the XNA metadata contract and the XNA IL provenance register. tools/api_compat/reference/BCL_PROVENANCE.md pins assembly mscorlib 4.0.0.0, file version 4.0.30319.1, 5196112 bytes, SHA-256 5634668d4775b0113f08ea31093b281fea69bfc4e99227f5ca761b4ed98acc63, CompanyName Microsoft Corporation, FileDescription Microsoft Common Language Runtime Class Library. tools/api_compat/build_bcl_inventory.rb admits it by exact SHA-256 and byte length, derives the public key token b77a5c561934e089 from the assembly own .publickey blob by the CLR rule rather than trusting a constant, checks the PE version resource, and proves the pairing: all ten pinned XNA assemblies declare an AssemblyRef to mscorlib naming exactly that version and token. It writes docs/generated/bcl-inventory.json with its own separate metrics, BCL_FAMILIES 3, BCL_TYPES 17, BCL_MEMBERS 246, BCL_EXCEPTION_TYPES 9. mscorlib is not an XNA assembly: REFERENCE_TYPES stays 257, REFERENCE_MEMBERS stays 2964, TYPES_WITH_IL stays 257 and TYPES_WITHOUT_IL stays 0. The inventory is demand-driven and aborts on a family the XNA reference contract does not name. No Microsoft-owned bytes, no IL text and no machine-local path is committed, and the gem packages zero Microsoft binaries

The Framework and Graphics assemblies are mixed-mode C++/CLI, so a native entry point is a P/Invoke declaration or an indirect calli through an unmanaged calling convention. 254 such methods make 77 of 257 reference types native-reachable over the assemblies own call graph. Foundation 22 measured 205 and 55 of 250 and Native frontier 2 corrected that to 214 and 61 of 257, by teaching the extractor to read a nested type declaration, which ikdasm indents inside its parent and closes with the short name, and a generic definition, which it declares as Name`1<T> and closes as Name`1. Native frontier 3 corrected it again, to 254 and 77, by removing a modopt blind spot: a mixed-mode C++/CLI thunk is declared .method public hidebysig static int32 modopt([mscorlib]...IsLong) Play(uint32), and the name reader took the first identifier before a parenthesis, so every such method was recorded as modopt while every call site resolved to its real name and every edge into it dangled. Sixteen reference types gained native reachability and none lost it, and no other measured number moved. The rule validates against the shipped boundary: every partial runtime type but GraphicsResource is native, and of the complete types exactly Input.Mouse, Input.GamePad, Graphics.Texture and FrameworkDispatcher are, each one a type whose native route this binding really implements. BEHAVIOR_EVIDENCE was retired and replaced by IL_UNAVAILABLE, NATIVE_RUNTIME and RUNTIME_DATA, which name what is genuinely absent

Foundation 23: TouchLocation and GestureSample; 2 types / 19 Ruby identities. Both constructors are pure storage with no validation; the three-argument TouchLocation form leaves prevState at the literal 0, which is Invalid; TryGetPreviousLocation fills its out value on both branches and answers [found, previousLocation]; Equals compares id, x, y, prevX and prevY while op_Equality compares all seven fields, a divergence preserved rather than normalised; every comparison is bne.un so NaN is never equal to itself; GetHashCode sums only id, x and y. GestureSample declares no Equals, GetHashCode, ToString or operator, so none is projected. No TouchPanel, TouchCollection, gesture recognition or touch device, and nothing produces either type

Foundation 31: TouchCollection and its nested TouchCollection+Enumerator, closed together because neither can be closed alone -- the declaring type's GetEnumerator returns the nested one and the nested one's Current and MoveNext call the declaring type's Item and Count; 2 types / 18 Ruby identities. The struct declares eight TouchLocation slots and an int32 count, never a list, which is the whole eight-location ceiling. The constructor throws ArgumentNullException(touches) for null and ArgumentOutOfRangeException(touches) for more than eight, sets isConnected to the literal true, and expands each element through TouchLocation.TryGetPreviousLocation, using TouchLocationState.Invalid and a zero previous position when there is none. IsReadOnly answers the literal true and Insert, RemoveAt, Add, Clear, Remove and the Item setter are each a two-instruction body that throws NotSupportedException, mapped by managed.not-supported-exception to CNA::Runtime::NotSupportedError so an ordinary rescue catches it. The indexer constructs ArgumentOutOfRangeException(index) in its own IL and therefore raises RangeError, unlike a forwarding indexer. IndexOf scans with op_Equality over all seven TouchLocation fields, Contains is that scan negated, CopyTo throws ArgumentNullException(array) and ArgumentOutOfRangeException(arrayIndex) twice over, and FindById answers the ordered pair [found, location] filling the CLR default TouchLocation on the false branch. GetEnumerator copies the collection struct, so the enumerator walks a snapshot; it starts at -1, Current forwards to the indexer with no guard so reading it before the first MoveNext or after exhaustion raises exactly what the indexer raises, MoveNext clamps position to Count, and Dispose has a bare ret body. IEnumerator.Reset is a private explicit interface implementation outside the selected surface and is not projected. Nothing produces a TouchCollection: no TouchPanel, no gesture recognition, no touch device, and the internal Update that XNA's input layer drives is not projected

Foundation 32: TouchPanel, 1 type / 14 Ruby identities, closing the Input.Touch namespace. A CLR abstract sealed class, projected under the static-class rule with new raising TypeError and made private, as FrameworkDispatcher already does. The entire pinned Input.Touch assembly is a stub on the Windows profile: not one of its methods reaches a native entry point, Touch.WindowHandle is a plain static field read, and TouchPanelCapabilities.GetCaps is initobj followed by ret, so every member is settled by IL rather than by a device. GetState is the one member that needed deriving: its IL zeroes a local XNAINPUT_TOUCH_LOCATION_STATE, may call the private OnDisplaySettingsChanged, calls the internal TouchCollection.Update, and assigns the never-filled local back over prevState, so both state structs are zeroed on every call for ever, Update adds nothing and stores the literal true connected flag, and the observable result is always an empty connected collection, which TouchCollection.new([]) produces with identical state. GetState().IsConnected true beside GetCapabilities().IsConnected false is not a contradiction: the first is a field of the returned value set by the non-throwing branch and the second is the member that reports device presence, and both are XNA's Windows answer. IsGestureAvailable and ReadGesture throw InvalidOperationException, newly mapped to RuntimeError, until EnabledGestures has been assigned, and ReadGesture throws again afterwards because no gesture is ever available; both messages are localized FrameworkResources strings that are not reproduced. EnabledGestures rejects an undefined bit through GestureType.coerce, which draws the identical boundary to the CLR's 0xfffffc00 mask because the declared bits sum to exactly 0x3FF, differing only in raising RangeError rather than ArgumentException. DisplayOrientation accepts exactly one declared value, never a combination, matching Helpers.ValidateOrientation. WindowHandle is a static IntPtr nothing on this profile consumes

Foundation 33: GameServiceContainer, 1 type / 4 Ruby identities, and the two BCL identities it was blocked on. The type is a managed container over one private Dictionary<Type, object>; the hash-admitted IL inventory records one public constructor, one declared field and no native reachability, so nothing in it touches CNA. Its constructor is public, so unlike most of the Game family a caller can make one and use it, but what it is for is Game.Services, and Game is one of the six deferred partial runtime types, so nothing in this binding registers a service. All three members open with the same null check throwing ArgumentNullException(type); AddService then throws ArgumentNullException(provider), ArgumentException naming type for a key already present, and ArgumentException naming no parameter when type.IsAssignableFrom(provider.GetType()) is false; RemoveService pops the Dictionary.Remove result so removing an absent key is harmless; GetService tests ContainsKey and otherwise loads null, so an absent service answers nil rather than raising. All four CLR messages are localized Resources strings and none is reproduced. System.Type projects to a Ruby Module, the type token Ruby has, which is what it is in all twenty-four places the XNA surface names it, and IsAssignableFrom is exactly is_a?. System.IServiceProvider is recorded in a new register, BclProjection::STRUCTURAL_COLLAPSE, as an identity that projects to no Ruby constant at all: it declares one member, GetService(Type), which the implementing type declares publicly, so the contract survives as that member and inventing a Ruby module would add an identity the CLR does not have. The API verifier asserts no constant was invented, and a mutation test proves the assertion fires

Foundation 24: AudioListener and AudioEmitter; 2 types / 11 Ruby identities. Both keep state in a native-layout XACT struct but call no native code. Every Vector3 passes through FlipHandedness, which is (X, Y, -Z), on both getter and setter; the constructor stores Position and Velocity unflipped so their first read answers a negative-zero Z, while Forward and Up are flipped at construction and read back exactly. DopplerScale is guarded by bge.un, so NaN is accepted and only an ordered negative value raises. No audio engine, SoundEffect, Microphone or XACT runtime is added and nothing set here is ever heard

Foundation 24: PresentationParameters; 13 Ruby identities. The constructor is base() plus exactly one store, set_IsFullScreen(true), so IsFullScreen defaults to true and every other field keeps its CLR default. No setter validates anything; Bounds is a fresh Rectangle derived from the back buffer; Clone copies the whole settings struct. DeviceWindowHandle keeps the existing System.IntPtr rule - a signed native-pointer-width Ruby Integer, never a Fiddle::Pointer. It creates no GraphicsDevice, looks up no native window, enumerates no adapter, builds no swap chain and presents nothing

Foundations 25 and 26: a CLR class whose only constructor is internal projects with new made private, as GraphicsResource and Texture already did, so public non-constructibility is part of the contract while the internal path stays reachable through __send__. DisplayMode, DisplayModeCollection, ResourceCreatedEventArgs and ResourceDestroyedEventArgs completed on that rule; 4 types / 11 Ruby identities. DisplayMode derives AspectRatio, which answers zero when either extent is zero, plus TitleSafeArea and a four-field ToString; DisplayModeCollection enumerates in order and Item[format] materialises a filtered list, without mixing in Ruby Enumerable. No producer is fabricated: GraphicsAdapter and the GraphicsDevice resource events stay absent

Foundation 27: the five ContentSerializer attributes; 16 Ruby identities. System.Attribute projects to the CNA::Runtime::Attribute marker base, designed because five otherwise unblocked types needed it. ContentSerializerAttribute stores allowNull true before calling the base constructor; CollectionItemName answers the literal Item whenever the raw field is null or empty and its setter throws ArgumentNullException, mapped to ArgumentError, for null or empty; HasCollectionItemName is the negation of that test; Clone copies the six raw fields. Foundation 46: CNA::Runtime::Dictionary and Microsoft.Xna.Framework.LaunchParameters, 1 XNA type / 1 Ruby identity over an eleventh projected BCL identity. The last purely-decisional BCL blocker, decided by measurement rather than preference. The admitted mscorlib settles how much of Dictionary`2 a projection owes: twenty-two of its methods are explicit interface implementations, which project to no member at all under the rule ReadOnlyCollection's twelve and Collection's fourteen already follow, and its SerializationInfo constructor is family. What is carried is the ordinary public surface -- Comparer, Count, Keys, Values, the indexer, Add, Clear, ContainsKey, ContainsValue, GetEnumerator, Remove, TryGetValue, GetObjectData and OnDeserialization -- plus the nested KeyCollection and ValueCollection, whose whole public surface is four members each. A Ruby Hash is the private store and never the public projection: Hash#[] answers nil where get_Item throws KeyNotFoundException, Hash#store overwrites where Add throws ArgumentException, and Hash#each never fails fast on a version counter. Measured exactly: the null-key refusal every keyed member shares, ContainsValue's separate null branch, Remove answering false without touching version, and Clear returning at its first branch so an empty Clear does not invalidate an enumeration. Bucket traversal order is deliberately not reproduced -- it is unspecified in the contract and the canonical C ABI's own launch-parameter enumeration sorts by name rather than trusting it -- while key equality, duplicate recognition, lookup, removal, Count and version invalidation are exact. The default comparer projects to nil because EqualityComparer<TKey>.Default is the key's own equality, which is Ruby's; a supplied comparer is a duck type answering Equals and GetHashCode, which is the whole of IEqualityComparer<T>, and no implementation-private CLR comparer class is exposed. GetObjectData and OnDeserialization take a named-value carrier: no formatter, surrogate selector, binder or stream format is invented, and SerializationInfo stays out of the register because the pinned reference never names it in a public signature. LaunchParameters declares one member, its public parameterless constructor, and parses ARGV with XNA's own rules -- leading / and - trimmed as a run, split on the FIRST colon, a colonless argument KEPT with String.Empty as its value, an empty key skipped, first occurrence winning. Game.LaunchParameters is one ldfld, created by the constructor, needing no native host. The canonical CNA launch-parameter routes are deliberately unbound: audited against this IL they skip a colonless argument, upsert where Add refuses, and enumerate sorted by name, all observable through the inherited surface. Nothing here serialises anything and no content, window or storage runtime is implied

Foundation 47: Game's Dispose(Boolean), Finalize and ShowMissingRequirementMessage(Exception), the three family members that were the whole of its remaining decisional surface. Dispose(Boolean) opens `ldarg.1; brfalse` straight to `ret`, so Dispose(false) does nothing and Finalize -- which is exactly that call in a try/finally around base.Finalize -- is observably a no-op; the two overloads project to one Ruby method dispatching on arity, widening the protected one to public as a recorded mapping limitation. The Monitor.Enter(this) that Foundation 41 recorded as a deviation is now taken, with ::Monitor rather than Mutex because the CLR lock is reentrant and a Disposed handler re-entering it must not deadlock. UnhookDeviceEvents is a genuine no-op rather than one made into one: its field is written only by HookDeviceEvents, which the producer audit deliberately omits. XNA's absent disposed flag remains a recorded deviation, because native destruction is not repeatable. ShowMissingRequirementMessage is host?.ShowMissingRequirementMessage(e) ?? false; GameHost's own body is an unconditional false and only WindowsGameHost overrides it with a System.Windows.Forms MessageBox, so answering false here is the abstract base's real behaviour and the truthful answer, not a stub -- and RunGame rethrows on false, so the exception still reaches the caller. The two catch clauses are wired and live: a subclass raising either projected requirement exception from a lifecycle callback reaches them, the default rethrows, an override answering true really suppresses, and an unrelated exception is not caught. RunGame's finally clearing inRun is now in Run, so the flag survives a run that ends by raising. This claims no finalizer, no ObjectSpace registration, no GC.SuppressFinalize analogue, no message box, no dialog and no CNA route

Foundation 44: Game.Tick, bound to cna_game_tick, the frame step cna_game_run_one_frame wraps. The pinned Game.dll IL makes the split XNA's own -- Game.RunOneFrame is host?.RunOneFrame(), and WindowsGameHost implements that as gameWindow.Tick(), then GameHost.OnIdle() whose only subscriber is Game.HostIdle whose whole body is this.Tick(), then the Guide-visibility relay -- so the two are bound separately and a regression test asserts they never become aliases. Tick's first instruction, if (ShouldExit) return, is projected in managed state because exitRequested is written exactly once in the whole assembly, by Game.Exit, and never cleared, while CNA's step after cna_game_request_exit still delivers one Update. Measured faithful over the reviewed artifact: the fixed step advances TotalGameTime by exactly one TargetElapsedTime per tick, a pending SuppressDraw skips exactly one draw, and Tick delivers no lifecycle callback other than Update/BeginDraw/Draw/EndDraw. Recorded deviations: CNA refuses a frame step from inside a lifecycle callback, which surfaces as its own translated error, and the route is owner-thread bound. Two CNA loop deviations were measured and deliberately not re-implemented on the managed side -- the missing doneFirstUpdate draw gate and the missing priming Update in Run -- because the native Game owns the loop and a managed copy would double a step CNA performs

Foundation 29 resolved the decision mapping.readonly-collection recorded. System.Collections.ObjectModel.ReadOnlyCollection`1 projects to CNA::Runtime::ReadOnlyCollection, a dedicated runtime support class, and never to Array, a frozen Array, Enumerable alone, Set or an opaque Object. The mscorlib IL admitted by reference.bcl-authority settles the design rather than taste: the CLR constructor stores the IList<T> reference and all six public read members forward one call to it, so the wrapper is a live view whose Count and contents follow the backing list, and a frozen copy would be a different type; none of the six validates anything of its own; and read-only is a property of the interface, expressed by twelve explicit interface implementations that throw NotSupportedException unconditionally, which Ruby projects as the absence of any mutating member. Ruby has class inheritance, so an XNA class whose CLR base is this generic inherits from the support class; because a Ruby class is not statically generic the CLR type argument is carried as class metadata via projects_elements and measured by the API verifier under GENERIC_MAPPING_MISMATCH. The class carries one language-support identity of its own, each, and includes Enumerable, every method of which Ruby derives from each alone; CLR identities are PascalCase or operators and language support is not, so the two can never be confused. The projection completes no XNA type: GraphicsAdapter drops to NATIVE_RUNTIME alone and Media.VisualizationData to RUNTIME_DATA alone, while Microphone keeps System.Byte[] and SpriteFont keeps System.Char, Nullable`1[System.Char] and StringBuilder

The canonical C ABI already exposes the whole GraphicsAdapter surface (count, info, description, device name, current mode, supported modes, device preferences, profile support and both format negotiations), so no ABI expansion is needed to reach it. What the qualified artifact cannot supply is truthful data: libcna_c_api.so 0.7.0 was linked with the HEADLESS platform, carrying no SDL2 or SDL3 platform, so CNA GetDisplays answers nothing and the native adapter falls back to a synthetic entry described as Default Display with a single 800x480 mode. Binding a Ruby GraphicsAdapter to that would publish invented hardware. The C ABI additionally refuses the native monitor handle by design, returning CNA_RESULT_NOT_SUPPORTED, and answers every adapter query only through a callback-scoped graphics-device handle, while XNA Adapters and DefaultAdapter are statics usable before any device exists

Foundation 30 resolved the decision mapping.not-supported-exception recorded. System.NotSupportedException maps to CNA::Runtime::NotSupportedError, a dedicated language-support class descending from StandardError. Ruby NotImplementedError is deliberately refused: it descends from ScriptError, not StandardError, so a bare rescue -- the analogue of a CLR catch (Exception) -- does not catch it, and a routine recoverable CLR failure would escape ordinary Ruby error handling; RuntimeError and ArgumentError are catchable but each say something the CLR exception does not and neither carries a distinct identity a caller can rescue by name. The admitted mscorlib settles the hierarchy, NotSupportedException under SystemException under System.Exception, which the register already roots at StandardError, and the three public constructor shapes, with the message forwarded and never synthesised; the parameterless form's CLR message is the localized framework resource Arg_NotSupportedException, which is not reproduced, so a NotSupportedError raised without a message carries Ruby's own default. The mapping lives in a third register, BclProjection::THROWN_EXCEPTIONS, kept separate from TYPES and EXCEPTION_BASES because a thrown exception is never named by an XNA public signature and must not count as a mapped BCL identity on the dependency frontier. The API verifier resolves every entry and reports LANGUAGE_MAPPING_MISMATCH for one that is not a class, is not a StandardError, or descends from ScriptError; five mutations are covered by test, including the NotImplementedError substitution
